idea: Replace the random-order baseline with a target-similarity filter plus dedup. Steps: (1) Fit a TfidfVectorizer on char n-grams (analyzer='char_wb', ngram_range=(1,3), sublinear_tf=True, max_features ~50k) over the first 2000 chars of each pool doc plus the target_sample; train a LogisticRegression (C=1) with positives = target_sample (200) plus pool docs that match the obvious WikiText format heuristic (starts with '= ' and first line ends with ' =', contains ' @-@ ' or ' , ' tokenised punctuation), negatives = a seeded random sample of 3000 pool docs not matching the heuristic; score every pool doc with predict_proba. (2) Drop exact and near duplicates: keep the first occurrence by hash of whitespace-normalised, lowercased first 500 chars. (3) Drop junk: docs shorter than 200 chars, docs with <70% of characters in letters/space, or with spam markers ('Click here to order', 'best price guaranteed', 'coupon'). (4) Rank surviving docs by score, take those with probability > 0.5 (the wiki-style articles); count their tokens with tiktoken gpt2. If they hold fewer than T tokens, do NOT pad with off-domain text: return just this set, shuffled with CURATE_SEED, so the trainer cycles it. If more than T, keep the top-scoring ones up to T tokens and shuffle.
why: The pool is visibly a mix of WikiText-style articles (the target) with spam, code, forum and web text, so spending all T tokens on deduplicated in-domain articles, even with repetition, should lower held-out bpb far more than training on roughly half off-domain junk.
outcome: dev 1.9455 against 1.9633 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea:
Add a word-order damage filter for the wiki-format docs that the current pipeline lets through. The pool sample shows articles with a valid '= Title =' header but a shuffled body ('the , , The of that Grand May One as ...'). Char n-grams and the format heuristic cannot see this, so these docs are currently both selected and used as classifier positives.

Implementation:
1. Build a word-bigram reference from target_sample. Split on whitespace, lowercase, and map every word outside the 300 most frequent target words to '<w>' (keep punctuation tokens as they are). Count bigrams and unigrams with add-0.1 smoothing.
2. For each doc, compute the mean bigram log-probability log P(w2|w1) over the first 400 tokens after the header line.
3. Add cheap auxiliary rates per doc: the fraction of adjacent punctuation-punctuation pairs such as ', ,' ', .' '. ,', and the fraction of '. ' tokens followed by a capitalised word.
4. Calibrate on the target sample. Compute the same score on each of the 200 target docs, and also on seeded word-shuffled copies of them as synthetic negatives. Set the threshold at the midpoint between the 2nd percentile of clean target scores and the 98th percentile of shuffled-copy scores. If the two overlap, fall back to the 2nd percentile of clean scores.
5. Drop every pool doc below the threshold. Do this before choosing classifier positives, so shuffled docs no longer count as positives, and before dedup, so that a clean copy survives instead of a shuffled first occurrence.
6. Apply the same calibrated test with shuffled-within-line and character-noised synthetic negatives (random 10% character substitutions), using the out-of-vocabulary rate against the target and pool vocabulary, to catch other damage types.

Keep the rest of the pipeline unchanged: P > 0.5, no off-domain padding, seeded shuffle.
why: Word-shuffled wiki articles pass the char n-gram classifier and the format heuristic, so part of the T token budget is probably going to text with destroyed word order, and replacing it with clean in-domain text should lower bpb.
outcome: dev 1.8243 against 1.9455 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea:
Extend the damage, junk and dedup checks from the document head to the whole document. At present the damage filter scores only the first 400 tokens after the header, junk checks read the first 5000 chars, and dedup hashes the first 500 chars.

1. Damage filter over several windows. For each pool doc, score up to 6 evenly spaced 400-token windows covering the body: always the first and the last, plus interior ones. Docs under 800 tokens get one or two windows. Compute the same four scores per window (bigram log-prob, punct-punct rate, dot-capital rate, OOV rate). Drop the doc if any window fails any active test.

2. Recalibrate for the stricter rule. Take the same multi-window scores on the 200 target docs (leave-one-out) and on their synthetic negatives. Use each clean target doc's minimum window score as the clean distribution. Use single-window scores of the negatives as the negative distribution. Set the threshold at the midpoint between the 1st percentile of the clean minima and the 98th percentile of the negatives, with the same fallback and switch-off logic as now. This keeps the false-drop rate on clean docs at about 1-2% per test.

3. Whole-doc junk check. Search the full lowercased text for the spam markers. Compute the letter ratio on three 3000-char slices (start, middle, end) and reject the doc if any slice is below 0.70.

4. Stronger dedup. In addition to the head key, compute an md5 of the normalised 500 chars taken from the middle of the doc, for docs over 3000 chars. Treat a doc as a duplicate if either its head key or its middle key has already been seen among kept docs.

Everything else stays unchanged: the classifier, P > 0.5, no off-domain padding, seeded shuffle. Keep the runtime under the limit by reusing the tokenisation memo and scoring in chunks.
why: Docs that are shuffled, noised, spam-spliced or duplicated only after their first 400 tokens currently pass every check and are trained on (and cycled), so screening the whole doc should remove the remaining corrupted in-format tokens that the last experiment showed to be very costly.
outcome: dev 1.8327 against 1.8243 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Tighten the damage filter so it also catches mild or partial damage. Calibrate each test on the clean target docs only, instead of at the midpoint between clean docs and heavily damaged synthetic copies.

1. Keep the four existing scores, on the same first-400-token window and with the same leave-one-out scoring of the 200 target docs: bigram log-prob, punct-punct rate, dot-capital rate, OOV rate.
2. Change the threshold for each test to the 5th percentile of the clean leave-one-out scores (higher = cleaner, so drop docs below it). The synthetic negatives no longer set the threshold. Use them only as a sanity check: keep a test active only if at least 90% of its synthetic negatives fall below the clean 5th percentile; otherwise switch it off.
3. Add two clean-calibrated scores from the same window: (a) the fraction of alphabetic tokens that are all lowercase, as a two-sided test that drops docs outside the clean 2.5th to 97.5th percentile range, to catch case-mangled text; (b) the distinct-token ratio (unique tokens / tokens), dropping docs below the clean 2.5th percentile, to catch repeated or looped text.
4. Add a mean-token-length test over whitespace tokens, two-sided at the clean 1st and 99th percentiles, to catch deleted or inserted spaces.

Leave everything else unchanged: damaged docs are excluded from classifier positives and from dedup first-occurrences, P > 0.5, no off-domain padding, seeded shuffle. Losing about 15% of clean docs is acceptable, since the trainer cycles the selected set anyway.
why: The midpoint thresholds were set against 100% shuffles and 10% character noise, so lightly damaged docs (local or partial shuffles, low-rate noise, case or spacing damage) probably still pass, and a clean-percentile cut removes them at the cost of a few clean docs.
outcome: dev 1.8501 against 1.8243 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
When the selected clean wiki set holds fewer than T tokens (W < T), fill the shortfall with clean general-English prose from the pool instead of letting the trainer cycle the wiki set. Finish the token stream on pure wiki text.

1. Keep the current pipeline unchanged to obtain the wiki set S (damage filter, classifier P > 0.5, dedup, junk) and its token count W. If W >= T, return exactly what the current code returns.

2. Filler candidates are pool docs not in S that fail the wiki heuristic and have P <= 0.5. Each must pass all of these:
   a. Existing junk and spam checks, existing dedup, and length >= 500 chars.
   b. Re-tokenise the first 4000 chars with the regex `\w+|[^\w\s]`, so punctuation is split off as in the target. Then apply the existing calibrated OOV test and bigram log-prob test, with the same thresholds. This drops character-scrambled and word-shuffled prose.
   c. Function-word rate: the fraction of tokens that are among the 50 most frequent alphabetic target words must be at least the 2nd percentile of the same rate over the 200 target docs. This drops code, keyword spam and lists.
   d. The fraction of chars in `{}<>;=_\$/` must be under 1%. This drops code and markup.

3. Rank the candidates by mean bigram log-prob under the target model, most target-like first. Take them in that order until the filler reaches F = min(T - W, W) tokens, counted with tiktoken. This keeps wiki at half the stream or more.

4. Ordering. Shuffle S with the seed. Reserve the last ~30% of S by tokens as the tail. Shuffle the filler together with the other 70% of S, using the seed, to form the head. Return head + tail, so the final part of training is pure target-domain text. If W + F < T, the trainer cycles this list as before.

Add a comment giving W/T and the number of filler docs, so the outcome can be interpreted.
why: Experiment 4 lost about 15% of clean docs and got 0.026 bpb worse, which suggests the wiki set is below T and unique data is the constraint, so clean prose may teach more general English than repeated wiki passes while a wiki-only tail keeps the model tuned to the target format.
outcome: dev 1.8479 against 1.8243 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Make the target classifier header-independent and self-trained, so clean wiki-style docs that lack a '= Title =' first line (section fragments, articles starting mid-text, docs with a stray line before the header) are no longer used as negatives or scored down.

1. Round 1: run the current classifier unchanged to get p1 for every pool doc.

2. Round 2: build a body text per doc. Strip leading lines until the first line that is not a '= ... =' header, using the existing _body logic, then take the next 2000 chars (same budget cap as now). Do the same for target_sample. Fit a new TfidfVectorizer (char_wb, 1-3, sublinear_tf, 50k features) on these bodies.
   - Positives: the 200 target bodies, plus up to 5000 seeded-sampled pool docs with ok[i] and p1 > 0.9.
   - Negatives: up to 3000 seeded-sampled pool docs with p1 < 0.1 that also fail the wiki heuristic. Docs with p1 in [0.1, 0.9] are left unlabeled. Damaged docs (ok False) are in neither class.
   - Fit LogisticRegression(C=1, max_iter=300) and score all pool bodies to get p2.

3. Final score = max(p1, p2). Select with score > 0.5 as now. The damage filter (ok), dedup and junk checks still apply to every selected doc, including the newly admitted headerless ones. Everything else is unchanged: best-first up to T tokens, seeded shuffle, no off-domain padding.

4. Fallback: if round 2 has fewer than 50 negatives or raises, use p1 alone.

5. Add a comment or debug variable recording how many docs and tokens are selected by p1 alone and by max(p1, p2), so we learn whether the wiki set is below T.

Stay within 180 s by reusing the tiktoken counting as is and capping the body prefix with the same VECTORISE_CHAR_BUDGET.
why: Tighter filters and off-domain filler both hurt, so the remaining gain is likely in recovering more clean in-domain text, and the current classifier labels headerless wiki docs as negatives and so probably excludes some of it.
outcome: dev 1.8294 against 1.8243 for the best at the time, rejected

why: Removing heavily shuffled docs gave the only large gain so far (0.12 bpb), and the current midpoint thresholds, calibrated only on fully damaged copies, probably let lightly or partially damaged wiki docs through; a detector trained on graded damage can catch those while losing only about 2% of clean docs.
outcome: dev 1.8398 against 1.8243 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add title-level dedup for wiki-format docs, keeping the cleanest copy of each article; everything else stays unchanged.

1. Title key. For every pool doc whose first non-empty line matches '= Title =' (a single '=' on each side, not '= = Section = ='), set the key to the title lowercased, whitespace-collapsed and stripped of non-alphanumeric characters. Docs without such a header get no key and are handled as now.

2. Expose per-doc scores. Have the damage filter also return the per-doc mean bigram log-prob that it already computes on the first-400-token window (NaN if not scored).

3. Pick one winner per title. Group docs by title key after the damage filter, the P > 0.5 test and the junk check. Docs that fail any of these never compete. Within a group of two or more:
   a. Drop any doc whose bigram score is more than 0.15 nats below the group's best score. This treats it as a mildly damaged copy of the same article, judged against its own clean twin instead of a global threshold.
   b. Among the rest, keep only the doc with the most characters, which favours the full article over truncated copies. Break ties by higher bigram score, then by lower index.
   If scores are NaN, use length alone.

4. Keep the existing head-hash dedup for docs without a title key, and as a first pass.

5. Do not change the classifier positives, the thresholds, the P > 0.5 rule, the no-padding rule or the seeded shuffle.

6. Add a debug comment or variable recording the number of title groups with more than one doc, the number of docs removed, and the final W/T, so the result can be interpreted.
why: The head-hash dedup misses copies of the same article that differ in their first 500 chars (truncated or mildly damaged twins), and comparing copies within a title removes them without the clean-doc losses that made the global tighter filters in experiments 4 and 7 worse.
outcome: dev 1.8254 against 1.8243 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Make the returned list cover the full T tokens explicitly, instead of relying on the trainer to cycle one fixed permutation. Everything upstream stays unchanged (damage filter, classifier, dedup, junk, P > 0.5, no off-domain padding).

1. Compute the selected set S and per-doc gpt2 token counts as now. Let W be the total tokens in S. For this step, count tokens for all of S rather than stopping at T.

2. If W < T: build the output as consecutive epochs. Each epoch is all of S in a fresh seeded permutation (rng derived from CURATE_SEED and the epoch number). Append epochs until the cumulative tokens reach T plus a small margin of about 2%. For the last, partial epoch, do not take a random prefix. Fill it with the docs of S ranked highest by mean bigram log-prob under the target model (the per-doc score the damage filter already computes; expose it), then shuffle that partial epoch. This way the extra repeats go to the cleanest, most target-like docs, and no batch order repeats between epochs.

3. If W >= T: do not take the top classifier scores (they are saturated near 1.0 and effectively arbitrary). Rank S by the same bigram log-prob score, drop the lowest-scoring docs until the remainder just covers T tokens, then shuffle with the seed. The surplus is spent on removing the most borderline docs.

4. Add a debug variable or comment recording W/T, the number of full epochs and the size of the partial epoch, so the result shows which regime the pool is in.

Keep the fallbacks: if the scores are NaN or unavailable, use the plain shuffle and the current behaviour.
why: Every rejected experiment changed which docs are selected, and each came out slightly worse, so this one keeps the selection and instead spends the token budget better — no repeated permutation when the set is cycled, and repeats or cuts decided by target-likeness rather than a saturated classifier score — though I expect the gain to be small.
outcome: dev 1.8329 against 1.8243 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add a gross-splice check on the later parts of each document, with near-zero false drops on clean docs. Experiment 3 bundled this with stricter recalibrated thresholds that also dropped clean docs; this version only removes docs whose middle or end is clearly off-domain or clearly destroyed. Head tests, thresholds, classifier training, dedup, P > 0.5, no padding and the seeded shuffle all stay unchanged.

1. Candidates: only docs that would currently be selected (ok, P_head > 0.5, not junk, not a duplicate) and are longer than 6000 chars. Shorter docs are untouched.

2. Slices: for each candidate take a middle slice (2000 chars centred on len/2) and a tail slice (the last 2000 chars). Snap both to whitespace boundaries.

3. Domain test: transform both slices with the already fitted TfidfVectorizer and score them with the already fitted LogisticRegression. Do not retrain. Mark the doc bad if either slice has P(target) < 0.2. Also mark it bad if any spam marker occurs anywhere in the full lowercased text.

4. Destruction test: on the first 400 whitespace tokens of each slice, compute the existing bigram log-prob and OOV scores with the existing full-target model. Do not use the midpoint thresholds. Use the 'as bad as a synthetic negative' level instead: mark the doc bad only if the slice's bigram score is at or below the 98th percentile of the shuffled-negative calibration scores, or its OOV score is at or below the 98th percentile of the char-noise negatives. Have _damage_filter return these two values. If either value is unavailable, skip that test.

5. Safety valve: apply steps 3-4 to the 200 target docs (those over 6000 chars). If more than 3% of them are flagged, disable the whole check.

6. Remove flagged docs from the chosen set before token counting. Do not change which copy dedup keeps, and do not change the classifier positives.

7. Stay within the time limit: transform slices only for the candidates, in one batch of at most 2 x 2000 chars per doc. Skip the check if there are more than 12000 candidates.
why: Every current test reads only the document head, so long wiki articles with spliced-in spam or code or a shuffled later section still pass, and removing only the gross cases avoids the clean-doc losses that hurt experiments 3, 4 and 7.
outcome: dev 1.8303 against 1.8243 for the best at the time, rejected

why: Hand-designed tightening of the damage tests (experiments 4 and 7) cost clean docs and scored worse, whereas a gated two-sample test against the target sample removes documents only if the selected set contains a measurable non-target subpopulation, such as mild or unanticipated damage, and otherwise leaves the current best output unchanged.
outcome: dev 1.8276 against 1.8243 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Loosen the damage filter so it only drops docs that are about as damaged as the synthetic negatives, and keeps mildly damaged wiki docs. Everything else stays unchanged (classifier, dedup, junk, P > 0.5, no off-domain padding, seeded shuffle, head-only 400-token window).

1. In _threshold, when the clean and negative distributions separate (lo = 2nd percentile of clean scores > hi = max 98th percentile of the negatives), replace the midpoint 0.5*(lo+hi) with hi + 0.2*(lo - hi). Use a module constant THRESH_FRAC = 0.2. Apply this to all four tests: bigram log-prob, punct-punct rate, dot-capital rate, OOV rate.

2. When they overlap, keep the switch-off for the auxiliary tests b and c. For tests a and d, change the fallback from the 2nd percentile of clean scores to the 0.5th percentile (the minimum for 200 docs), so the fallback is also not stricter than necessary.

3. Docs that now pass the damage filter are treated exactly like other ok docs: eligible as classifier positives, eligible as dedup first-occurrences, and selected if P > 0.5.

4. Dedup preference. Because more mildly damaged copies now pass, choose which copy of a duplicate group (same head key) to keep by the highest mean bigram log-prob, the score the damage filter already computes (expose it; NaN counts as lowest; ties go to the lower index). This keeps the cleanest copy instead of the first.

5. Record in a debug variable the number of docs dropped by the damage filter under the old midpoint thresholds and under the new ones, and the final W/T, so the result can be interpreted.
why: Every stricter filter tried (experiments 3, 4, 7, 10) raised bpb, which suggests the clean wiki set is well under T and that mildly damaged in-domain articles are worth more than extra repeats, so moving the threshold toward the heavily damaged negatives should add useful in-domain tokens while still excluding fully shuffled or noised docs.
outcome: dev 1.8339 against 1.8243 for the best at the time, rejected
